title: Let nothing disturb you
hookLine: Teresa's bookmark: all things pass; God does not change; patience obtains all
tomorrow: why would someone slip out of the house at night, happy?

lines: A LINE ON THE LOCK SCREEN.
A SLIP OF PAPER IN A BOOK.
cards: Some people keep a line on their lock screen that they need to see over and over. Teresa of Avila had something like that: a few short lines on a slip of paper, small enough to keep between the pages of a book.
Tradition says one like it was found in her prayer book after she died. No title, no explanation. Just a few words in Spanish, enough to hold up a life.

teach.b: The question underneath: how do you stay steady when everything is changing? Teresa's lines begin: "Nada te turbe, nada te espante." Let nothing disturb you, nothing frighten you.

teach.h: ALL THINGS PASS. GOD DOES NOT.
teach.b: Then, in plain English: all things pass. God does not change. Patience obtains everything.
Whoever has God lacks nothing. God alone is enough. It doesn't promise that nothing upsetting will happen.

It says the upsetting thing will pass, and against all that passing, one thing stays put. The prophet Malachi has the same steadiness: "For I am the LORD, I change not." A neighbor tradition knows the first half well.
The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, says in Max Müller's translation: "All created things perish." Seeing that clearly, the verse says, is the way to purity.
Shared ground: steadiness starts by telling the truth that things pass.

One honest difference: Teresa sets the passing against a God who doesn't change, and rests there; this verse of the Dhammapada doesn't point to an unchanging God, and finds the way in seeing the passing itself.
Two traditions, each in its own words, and neither pretends that nothing ends.

how: Some Christians keep Teresa's lines on a card or bookmark, and in some communities they are sung as a short, repeated chant.

games.q: what does “let nothing disturb you” mean?
o: a sign hung on a door to ask for silence
steady lines: all things pass, God does not change
a rule that monks must never be interrupted

games.q: let nothing disturb you — tap the pairs.

s: let nothing disturb you means never feel upset
the likely reading. the lines give reasons to be steady: all things pass, God does not change.
a verse of the Dhammapada also says created things pass away
all created things perish, in Max Müller's translation.
Teresa's lines and the Dhammapada mean exactly the same thing
both say things pass; Teresa rests in a God who doesn't change, and this verse doesn't point to one.

games.q: your grandpa is moving out of the house he's lived in most of his life, and he's rattled. you want to steady him. what does Teresa's bookmark offer?
o: a promise that nothing will really change.
all things pass, and in Teresa's lines, God does not.
a reminder that being upset shows weak faith.
games.why: Teresa doesn't promise nothing will hurt. all things pass; God does not change; patience obtains everything.

practice: If there's paper nearby, copy the lines out slowly by hand: let nothing disturb you, nothing frighten you; all things pass; God does not change; patience obtains everything; whoever has God lacks nothing; God alone is enough.
If not, say them inwardly, one line for each slow breath. When one line catches, stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Let nothing disturb you. Teresa's few lines: all things pass, God does not change, God alone is enough.

orig.note: Teresa's Spanish, written in the Latin alphabet: let nothing disturb you.

carryVoice: Here's your line: all things pass, and in Teresa's lines, God does not. Until next time.
